record.original_question: If a natural Hamiltonian system with a nonconstant potential on a flat two-torus T 2 (i.e., g has zero curvature ) admits a polynomial integral of odd degree, then it admits a linear integral. If it admits a nontrivial in tegral of even degree, then it admits a nontrivial quadratic integral. As explained above, the cases d = 3, 4, 5 of this conjecture were proved in [12, 1, 171, 59]. If the potential U is a trigonometric polynomial, the problem was solved by N. Denisova an d V. Kozlov in [58]. Analogs of Conjectures 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 are also interesting if the metric g is semi-Riemannian (i.e., an indefinite metric of signature (1, 1)), which, of course, implies that our surface is a torus or a Klein bottle. Note that semi-Riemannian metrics on T 2 whose geodesic flows admit integrals which are linear or quadratic in momenta were described in [163] and, combining this re sult with [28], one obtains a description of all natural Hamiltonian systems on semi-Riemannian 2- tori with linear and quadratic integrals. As seen from the discussion above, in the case of the sphere S2, almost nothing is known about integrals of degree d ≥ 5, which suggests the following open problem:

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda$ be a flat two-torus equipped with a flat Riemannian metric $g$ (zero Gaussian curvature), and let $U: T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth nonconstant potential. Consider the natural Hamiltonian system on the cotangent bundle $T^*T^2$ with Hamiltonian
$$H(x,p) = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{ij}(x) p_i p_j + U(x).$$
An integral of the system is a smooth function $F: T^*T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $\{H,F\}=0$; it is said to be polynomial of degree $d$ in momenta if $F(x,p) = \sum_{k=0}^{d} a_{i_1\cdots i_k}(x)\, p^{i_1}\cdots p^{i_k}$ with the top-degree component not identically zero. Such an $F$ is called nontrivial if it is functionally independent of $H$.

Prove or disprove the following:
(a) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of odd degree $d$, then it admits a nontrivial integral linear in momenta.
(b) If the system admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of even degree $d$, then it admits a nontrivial integral quadratic in momenta.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture is established only in low-degree cases: $d=3,4,5$ are proved, and the case of trigonometric-polynomial potentials is settled by Denisova–Kozlov. The general case for arbitrary degree remains open as of recent literature on polynomial integrals of natural systems on the 2-torus.

status_evidence.title: Fourth-degree polynomial integrals of a natural mechanical system on a two-dimensional torus
status_evidence.snippet: Result for degree d=4 on the 2-torus.
status_evidence.claim: Degree-4 case has been resolved in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Kozlov, polynomial integrals on the 2-torus
status_evidence.snippet: Existence of integrals of degree n implies an additional integral of degree 1 or 2, proved for n=3 and under spectral assumptions for n=4,5,6.
status_evidence.claim: Partial results exist; general conjecture is unresolved.
